items.title: Univalent holomorphic functions
The normalized univalent class on the unit disc
The extremal family of disc-valued univalent maps fixing a basepoint
A proper homologically simply connected plane domain has a bounded univalent competitor
items.strategy: Choose a point outside the domain, take a holomorphic square root of the translated coordinate by the published root theorem on homologically simply connected domains, use the open mapping theorem to show its image misses a disc, invert into the unit disc, and finally normalize the chosen basepoint with a Blaschke factor.

items.title: The extremal derivatives are positive and have a finite supremum
items.strategy: Positivity is built into the normalization. A small closed disc around the basepoint lies in the domain, so Cauchy estimates bound every competitor's derivative there; nonemptiness supplies a positive lower witness.

items.title: A maximizing sequence has a locally uniform limit with extremal derivative
items.strategy: Under the Axiom of Choice, choose a maximizing sequence in the extremal family. Since every competitor maps into the unit disc, the Choice-dependent Montel theorem gives a locally uniformly convergent subsequence, and derivative continuity transfers the supremal derivative to the limit.

items.title: A nonconstant locally uniform limit of univalent functions is univalent
items.strategy: Fix one point and divide the difference quotient by the linear factor that carries the unique zero. The resulting holomorphic functions are nowhere zero, so Hurwitz forces the limit quotient to be either identically zero or nowhere zero; the nonconstant case leaves at most one preimage for each value.

items.title: The extremal limit is univalent
items.strategy: The limit from the maximizing sequence has nonzero derivative at the basepoint, so it is nonconstant. Apply the univalent-limit lemma to the convergent subsequence.

items.title: An extremizer onto a proper subdomain of the disc can be enlarged
items.strategy: If the image omits a disc value, move that value to zero with a Blaschke factor, take a holomorphic square root of the resulting nowhere-zero map on the original domain, normalize back into the disc, and compare derivatives via the strict Schwarz lemma to contradict extremality.

items.title: Every proper homologically simply connected plane domain is conformally equivalent to the unit disc
items.strategy: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, build the extremal family, use Montel to attain its derivative supremum, prove the extremizer univalent, and prove it surjective by the square-root enlargement argument. The resulting bijective holomorphic map is the desired conformal equivalence.

items.title: The normalized Riemann map is unique
items.strategy: Compose one normalized Riemann map with the inverse of another to obtain a disc automorphism fixing the origin with positive derivative there. Schwarz rigidity forces that automorphism to be the identity.

items.title: The area theorem for exterior univalent functions
items.strategy: For each image circle, use real analyticity and regularity to construct an explicit finite elementary Green decomposition of its bounded side. Apply the licensed boundary-area formula, expand the Laurent series termwise, and compare nonnegative area with the coefficient sum.

items.title: The second coefficient of a normalized univalent function has modulus at most two
items.strategy: Apply the area theorem to the exterior map built from the odd square-root symmetrization of a normalized univalent function and read off the first Laurent coefficient.

items.title: Every normalized univalent disc map contains the quarter disc
items.strategy: If a point is omitted from the image, compose with the corresponding affine correction to get another normalized univalent function. Applying the second-coefficient bound to that corrected map forces the omitted point to have modulus at least one quarter.

items.title: Koebe's distortion theorem
items.strategy: At an arbitrary point z, precompose with the disc automorphism carrying 0 to z and affinely renormalize the result. Apply the sharp second-coefficient bound to this normalized univalent map and to its rotations to obtain the corresponding pre-Schwarzian inequality; integrate it along the radial segment to get (1-|z|)/(1+|z|)^3 <= |f'(z)| <= (1+|z|)/(1-|z|)^3.

items.title: Koebe's growth theorem
items.strategy: Integrate the upper derivative-distortion bound along the radial segment for the upper estimate. For the lower estimate, choose a point z_0 on |z|=r minimizing |f|, lift the segment from 0 to f(z_0) through the univalent inverse, use the lower derivative-distortion bound along that lifted curve, and integrate its radial variation to obtain r/(1+r)^2 <= |f(z_0)| and hence the bound at every point of the circle.

items.title: A quarter-disc inclusion at every point of a univalent disc map
items.strategy: Translate the chosen point to the origin with a Blaschke factor, normalize by the derivative, apply Koebe's quarter theorem, and undo the normalization.

items.title: Choice strength used in the extremal proof of the Riemann mapping theorem
The normalized Riemann map from the upper half-plane sending i to 0
items.strategy: Write the Cayley transform explicitly, adjust by a unimodular factor so the derivative at i is positive, and verify the normalization directly.

items.title: A normalized Riemann map for a horizontal strip
items.strategy: Send the strip to the upper half-plane by the exponential, then to the disc by a Cayley transform, and finally normalize the chosen basepoint by a disc automorphism.

items.title: A normalized Riemann map for a sector with an explicit branch choice
items.strategy: Choose the power-map branch sending the sector to a half-plane, compose with a Cayley transform to the disc, and normalize the specified interior point.

items.title: A normalized Riemann map for the slit plane
items.strategy: Use the principal root branch to send the slit plane to a sector, then compose with a half-plane-to-disc map and the final normalization at the chosen basepoint.

items.title: The extremal problem on the unit disc is solved by the identity map
items.strategy: Apply Schwarz's lemma to every disc automorphism fixing the origin and check that the identity realizes the maximal derivative one.

items.title: The Koebe function shows the quarter-disc constant is sharp
items.strategy: Handle w=0 directly, then solve the quadratic for w≠0 to compute the Koebe image as the plane slit along (-∞,-1/4]. Verify that -1/4 is omitted and approached, and compare with Koebe's quarter theorem.

items.title: The punctured disc is not biholomorphic to the unit disc
items.strategy: Extend the bounded inverse map from the punctured disc across zero. The open mapping theorem keeps the extended value inside the unit disc, and continuity of the inverse identity then forces the original biholomorphism to take the forbidden value zero.

items.title: FALSE: the Riemann map is unique without normalization
items.strategy: Compose any one Riemann map with a nontrivial disc automorphism; the result is another conformal equivalence with the same source and target but different normalization.

items.title: FALSE: a conformal equivalence preserves Euclidean area
items.strategy: The linear map z -> z/2 is a biholomorphism from the unit disc onto the radius-one-half disc, and those domains have different Euclidean areas.

title: Bloch, Schottky, and the Picard Theorems

items.title: Bloch radii and the Bloch constant
Landau radii and the Landau constant
Families of holomorphic functions omitting two common finite values
Maximizing-point rescaling produces a normalized map with uniformly bounded derivative
items.strategy: Fix R = 1/2 and maximize (R - |z|)|f'(z)| on the closed disc |z| <= R. If z_0 is a maximizer and r = (R - |z_0|)/2, then the affine normalization g(w) = (f(z_0 + rw) - f(z_0))/(r f'(z_0)) satisfies g(0) = 0, g'(0) = 1, and |g'(w)| <= 2 on the unit disc. Moreover r|f'(z_0)| is at least R|f'(0)|/2. This is a compact maximizing-point argument and uses neither a disc automorphism nor Ahlfors' lemma.

items.title: Controlled derivative oscillation forces injectivity on a fixed subdisc
items.strategy: For a normalized g with g(0)=0, g'(0)=1, and |g'|<=2, apply Schwarz to (g'-1)/3 to obtain |g'(w)-1|<=3|w|. On |w|<=1/6 this is at most 1/2, so straight-line integration makes g injective there and gives |g(w)|>=|w|/2 on its boundary. Rouche's theorem then puts the round disc of radius 1/12 inside g(D(0,1/6)); hence that disc is covered by a univalent restriction.

items.title: Bloch's theorem
items.strategy: Apply the maximizing-point rescaling with R=1/2 and the quantitative univalence lemma. Undoing the affine normalization yields a schlicht disc of radius at least (R/2)(1/12)=1/48 when |f'(0)|=1, which is a universal positive lower bound for the Bloch radius.

items.title: Landau's theorem
items.strategy: Every schlicht disc supplied by Bloch's theorem is in particular a round disc in the image. Taking the universal lower bound from Bloch therefore gives the Landau radius bound.

items.title: Disc functions omitting 0 and 1 admit holomorphic logarithms for f and 1-f
items.strategy: The unit disc is star-shaped and hence homologically simply connected. Apply the published logarithm theorem to the nowhere-zero holomorphic functions f and 1-f.

items.title: Schottky's theorem
items.strategy: Use a logarithm f=exp(2 pi i h); because h omits 0 and 1, take holomorphic square roots u^2=h and v^2=h-1, then a logarithm g of u-v. The identities (u-v)(u+v)=1 and u=cosh(g) give f=-exp(pi i cosh(2g)). The classical omitted lattice for g meets every open disc of radius 1. Rescaled Bloch therefore bounds |g'(w)| by the reciprocal of the distance to the unit-circle boundary. A center bound on |f(0)| bounds a suitable choice of |g(0)| (apply the same construction to 1-f when f(0) is small); radial integration bounds g on every smaller disc, and the displayed formula then bounds f there.

items.title: Families omitting two values are chordally normal
items.strategy: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, use Schottky's theorem locally on f, 1/f, or 1/(1-f), according to the center value, to obtain chordal equicontinuity. The Choice-dependent meromorphic Arzela-Ascoli criterion then gives normality.

items.title: Little Picard theorem
items.strategy: If an entire function omitted 0 and 1, then Schottky's theorem would bound it on every fixed disc by a constant depending only on its value at the origin. Letting the disc radius grow shows the function is bounded on the whole plane, so Liouville makes it constant.

items.title: Two omitted finite values rule out an essential singularity
items.strategy: Following Simonic Theorem 14, choose dyadic radii tending to the puncture and rescale the function to the fixed annulus 1/2 < |z| < 2. Montel-Caratheodory gives a chordally locally uniform subsequence. Its holomorphic-input chordal limit is either finite holomorphic or identically infinity. In the finite case the rescaled functions are uniformly bounded on the unit circle; in the infinity case their reciprocals are uniformly bounded there. The corresponding selected circles tend to the puncture, and the boundary maximum-modulus principle on every intervening annulus makes either f or 1/f bounded throughout a punctured neighborhood. The removable-singularity characterization then makes f removable or a pole, ruling out an essential singularity without any Zalcman or nonconstant-limit extraction.

items.title: Great Picard theorem
items.strategy: If two finite values were omitted near an essential singularity, the omitted-values lemma would force the singularity to be removable or a pole. For the infinitely-often clause, if a nonexceptional value occurred only finitely many times, shrink to a smaller punctured disc omitting that value and the exceptional one, and apply the same lemma again.

items.title: A nonconstant meromorphic function on the plane omits at most two sphere values
items.strategy: Move three distinct omitted sphere values to 0, 1, and infinity by a Möbius transformation. The transformed function is entire and omits 0 and 1, contradicting little Picard.

items.title: A meromorphic essential singularity omits at most two sphere values
items.strategy: Move the possible omitted sphere values to 0 and infinity with a Möbius transformation and apply the holomorphic great Picard theorem in the finite chart.

items.title: Agreement between the classical and Nevanlinna proofs of Picard's theorems

title: Bloch, Schottky, and the Picard Theorems — Examples

items.title: The elementary Bloch proof on this page yields the explicit lower bound 1/48
items.strategy: Read the constants from the maximizing-point rescaling and quantitative-univalence proof: r|f'(z_0)| is at least 1/4 and the normalized image disc has radius 1/12, giving 1/48 after undoing the normalization.

items.title: Schottky's theorem applied to a disc map with center value 1/2
items.strategy: Specialize Schottky's bound to the center value 1/2 and a smaller radius, then spell out how the theorem's constant depends only on the chosen radius.

items.title: The exponential function omits exactly zero and shows little Picard is sharp
items.strategy: Use the exponential image and kernel formulas to prove that every nonzero value has a full logarithmic fiber while zero is omitted, then compare with little Picard.

items.title: The function e^(1/z) omits zero and takes every nonzero value infinitely often near the origin
items.strategy: Solve e^(1/z)=w by 1/z = log w + 2πik, excluding the at most one integer that makes the denominator zero, and observe that the remaining infinitely many points tend to the puncture. The exponential still omits zero.

items.title: The exponential function omits 0 and infinity as a meromorphic map on the plane
items.strategy: View e^z as a meromorphic function with no poles. Its image is C\{0}, so the omitted sphere values are exactly 0 and infinity.

items.title: FALSE: little Picard needs a boundedness hypothesis
items.strategy: Little Picard itself shows that an entire function omitting two finite values is constant, with no boundedness assumption. The point of the theorem is exactly that boundedness is not needed.

items.title: FALSE: a nonconstant meromorphic function on the plane omits at most one sphere value
items.strategy: Use the preceding exponential counterexample, which is meromorphic on C and omits both 0 and infinity while remaining nonconstant.
